title: Die alte Bettelfrau
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, Band 2, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 150. Text from Wikisource (twice proofread against the original). Fresh translation made directly from the German; 1857 spelling preserved (daß, gieng, fieng, Thür).
about: KHM 150 has no ending. An old beggar-woman warms herself at a boy's fire, her ragged clothes catch alight without her noticing, and the boy — who could have doused them — simply watches. The tale closes on the narrator's own reproach, put straight to the listener: he should have put it out, shouldn't he, wept enough tears to do it if there was no water at hand? Nothing is resolved; the fire and the question are left burning.

sentences.t: Es war einmal eine alte Frau, du hast wohl ehe eine alte Frau sehn betteln gehn?
sentences.l: There was once an old woman — you have surely before now seen an old woman go begging?
sentences.i: There was once an old woman — you will have seen an old woman go begging before now, surely?
sentences.n: The narrator turns and speaks to the reader directly (“du hast”), which happens almost nowhere else in these tales. “ehe” here is not the conjunction ‘before’ but the old adverb ‘formerly, before now’ (ehemals); “sehn” and “gehn” are the 1857 contracted spellings of sehen and gehen.

sentences.t: diese Frau bettelte auch, und wann sie etwas bekam, dann sagte sie „Gott lohn euch.“
sentences.l: this woman begged too, and when she got something, then she said “God reward you.”
sentences.i: This woman too went begging, and whenever she was given something she said, “God reward you.”
sentences.n: “wann” stands here in the older sense of wenn, ‘whenever.’ “Gott lohn euch” is a wish, not a statement: “lohn” is the old subjunctive of lohnen — may God repay you — the beggar’s standing thanks. The “euch” is the respectful old plural address.

sentences.t: Die Bettelfrau kam an die Thür, da stand ein freundlicher Schelm von Jungen am Feuer und wärmte sich.
sentences.l: The beggar-woman came to the door, there stood a friendly rascal of a boy by the fire and warmed himself.
sentences.i: The beggar-woman came to the door, and there by the fire stood a friendly young rascal warming himself.
sentences.n: “ein Schelm von Jungen” is the ‘an X of a Y’ pattern, as in English ‘a rogue of a boy’; the second noun goes into the dative. “Schelm” is affectionate here, a scamp rather than a villain.

sentences.t: Der Junge sagte freundlich zu der armen alten Frau, wie sie so an der Thür stand und zitterte, „kommt, Altmutter, und erwärmt euch.“
sentences.l: The boy said kindly to the poor old woman, as she stood so at the door and trembled, “come, old mother, and warm yourselves.”
sentences.i: The boy said kindly to the poor old woman, as she stood there at the door shivering, “Come, old mother, and warm yourself.”
sentences.n: “wie” here means ‘as, while.’ “kommt” and “erwärmt euch” are plural imperatives used as the respectful form to an elder — the same “euch” she used in her blessing. “Altmutter” is a plain old form of address to an old woman, not a word for a relative.

sentences.t: Sie kam herzu, gieng aber zu nahe ans Feuer stehn, daß ihre alten Lumpen anfiengen zu brennen, und sie wards nicht gewahr.
sentences.l: She came up, went however to stand too near to the fire, so that her old rags began to burn, and she did not become aware of it.
sentences.i: She came up, but went to stand too close to the fire, so that her old rags caught fire, and she never noticed.
sentences.n: “gieng … ans Feuer stehn” pairs a verb of motion with a bare infinitive — went to stand by the fire — an older construction. “wards” is “ward es,” the archaic preterite ward of werden with a clipped es; modern German would have “wurde es.” “gewahr werden” = to become aware of.

sentences.t: Der Junge stand und sah das, er hätts doch löschen sollen?
sentences.l: The boy stood and saw that, he ought after all to have put it out?
sentences.i: The boy stood and watched it — surely he ought to have put it out?
sentences.n: The narrator breaks in again: a statement punctuated as a question, with “doch” carrying the insistence, ‘surely.’ “löschen” is to quench, to put out.

sentences.t: Nicht wahr, er hätte löschen sollen?
sentences.l: Is it not so, he ought to have put it out?
sentences.i: Isn’t that so — he ought to have put it out?
sentences.n: “nicht wahr” is the all-purpose German tag question, ‘isn’t that so.’ Asking it twice in almost the same words is the tale pressing the reader rather than the boy.

sentences.t: Und wenn er kein Wasser gehabt hätte, dann hätte er alles Wasser in seinem Leibe zu den Augen herausweinen sollen,
sentences.l: And if he had had no water, then he ought to have wept all the water in his body out through his eyes,
sentences.i: And if he had had no water, then he ought to have wept out through his eyes every drop of water in his body,
sentences.n: “herausweinen” is heraus- plus weinen, coined for the occasion: to weep something out. The piled-up subjunctives (“gehabt hätte … hätte … sollen”) put the whole thing into a past that never happened.

sentences.t: das hätte so zwei hübsche Bächlein gegeben zu löschen.
sentences.l: that would have given, say, two pretty little brooks to put it out.
sentences.i: and that would have made two fine little brooks to quench it with.
sentences.n: “so” here is the loose spoken ‘why, about, say.’ And there the tale stops: no rescue, no punishment, no ending, only the question of what the boy ought to have done. That is exactly what the 1857 printing has — nothing is missing.

glossary.ehe: ehe — formerly, before now (older adverb, = ehemals); elsewhere the conjunction ‘before’
glossary.erwärmt: erwärmen — warm (yourselves) (imperative pl. erwärmt euch; also the past participle)
glossary.es: es — it (the impersonal subject, as in „Es war einmal“ = there was once)
glossary.jungen: der Junge — boy (dat. sg. Jungen; „ein Schelm von Jungen“ = a rascal of a boy)
glossary.lohn: lohnen — may (God) reward (old subjunctive; „Gott lohn euch“ = may God repay you)
